title: How a Receptor Loads a Switch

scenes.tts: How can binding outside a cell load a molecular switch inside it? Follow one membrane as the message crosses without the ligand crossing.
scenes.caption: How can binding outside a cell load a molecular switch inside it? Follow one membrane as the message crosses without the ligand crossing.
scenes.visual: Fill the frame with one horizontal membrane. Above it, a gold agonist block approaches a blue receptor marked on screen '7-pass GPCR'. Below, a gray GDP switch waits inside a purple G-alpha block. A large dashed question arrow crosses the membrane, while the agonist itself stops above it. The color map begins here and remains fixed: receptor blue, agonist gold, G-alpha purple, beta-gamma teal, GDP gray, GTP green.
scenes.narration: How can binding outside a cell load a molecular switch inside it? Follow one membrane as the message crosses without the ligand crossing.

scenes.visual: Hold the opening question at large size. The gold agonist bobs gently above the receptor, the GDP switch drifts below, and the dashed question arrow pulses. No answer appears.
Over the same moving membrane, show the title 'How a Receptor Loads a Switch' for two seconds. Keep the receptor and switch visible behind it, then dissolve only the title.

scenes.tts: A G protein coupled receptor, or G P C R, is one chain woven repeatedly through the membrane. Its outer pocket and inner face are physically connected. An agonist is a ligand that favors receptor activation. It settles into the pocket and favors an active shape. One cytoplasmic helix swings outward, opening a cavity below.
scenes.caption: A G-protein-coupled receptor, or GPCR, is one chain woven repeatedly through the membrane. Its outer pocket and inner face are physically connected. An agonist is a ligand that favors receptor activation. It settles into the pocket and favors an active shape. One cytoplasmic helix swings outward, opening a cavity below.
scenes.visual: Zoom into the blue receptor until its seven labeled bars fill most of the frame height. Trace one continuous blue chain through all bars. The gold agonist drops into the outer pocket. Small outer shifts propagate down the bundle; the bar labeled 'helix 6' swings outward below. The new cytoplasmic cavity opens as a high-contrast dashed outline.
scenes.narration: A G-protein-coupled receptor, or GPCR, is one chain woven repeatedly through the membrane. Its outer pocket and inner face are physically connected. An agonist is a ligand that favors receptor activation. It settles into the pocket and favors an active shape. One cytoplasmic helix swings outward, opening a cavity below.

scenes.tts: A membrane-bound G protein waits below as a trimer. Purple G alpha holds gray G D P. Teal beta-gamma stays pressed against it. In this resting arrangement, the switch is off. The G-alpha tail rises into the receptor cavity, bringing the whole trimer to the active receptor.
scenes.caption: A membrane-bound G protein waits below as a trimer. Purple Gα holds gray GDP. Teal βγ stays pressed against it. In this resting arrangement, the switch is off. The Gα tail rises into the receptor cavity, bringing the whole trimer to the active receptor.
scenes.visual: Carry the active receptor at the same location. Build a large purple G-alpha block with a fitted gray GDP tile and a teal beta-gamma pair beside it. Short lipid tethers keep both near the inner membrane. Label the assembled cartoon 'inactive'. Its narrow purple tail docks into the open receptor cavity; all pieces rise together rather than appearing as a new layout.
scenes.narration: A membrane-bound G protein waits below as a trimer. Purple Gα holds gray GDP. Teal βγ stays pressed against it. In this resting arrangement, the switch is off. The Gα tail rises into the receptor cavity, bringing the whole trimer to the active receptor.

scenes.tts: Docking changes G alpha's grip on G D P. The gray nucleotide leaves first. Green G T P can then occupy the empty site. The receptor has acted as an exchange factor, not as a source of G T P. It remains ready to load another G protein while agonist stays bound.
scenes.caption: Docking changes Gα's grip on GDP. The gray nucleotide leaves first. Green GTP can then occupy the empty site. The receptor has acted as an exchange factor, not as a source of GTP. It remains ready to load another G protein while agonist stays bound.
scenes.visual: Keep the docked complex large. The fitted gray GDP tile loosens, slides out, and drifts into the cytosol. Only after the pocket is visibly empty does a green GTP tile move in and click into place. Add a small label 'exchange factor' beside the blue receptor. A second inactive trimer approaches in the background to show catalysis without crowding the main action.
scenes.narration: Docking changes Gα's grip on GDP. The gray nucleotide leaves first. Green GTP can then occupy the empty site. The receptor has acted as an exchange factor, not as a source of GTP. It remains ready to load another G protein while agonist stays bound.

scenes.tts: G T P changes the G-alpha surface and frees beta-gamma to engage targets. The textbook picture draws them apart. Activated G I may instead rearrange without fully separating. Either way, both surfaces can regulate effectors. Hydrolysis later returns G alpha to G D P and favors reassembly.
scenes.caption: GTP changes the Gα surface and frees βγ to engage targets. The textbook picture draws them apart. Activated Gi may instead rearrange without fully separating. Either way, both surfaces can regulate effectors. Hydrolysis later returns Gα to GDP and favors reassembly.
scenes.visual: Transform the docked complex into two adjacent signaling surfaces: purple G-alpha-GTP and teal beta-gamma. First show the canonical separation with a label 'textbook picture'. Then bring them near again under 'Gi may rearrange' without implying universal behavior. Both extend arrows toward unlabeled target shapes. Finally, the green tile turns gray and the trimer closes again in a small cycle inset.
scenes.narration: GTP changes the Gα surface and frees βγ to engage targets. The textbook picture draws them apart. Activated Gi may instead rearrange without fully separating. Either way, both surfaces can regulate effectors. Hydrolysis later returns Gα to GDP and favors reassembly.

scenes.tts: Now the cell chooses what those surfaces meet. Follow the hourglass. Many receptors narrow to a few G-alpha families and beta-gamma, then widen toward enzymes and channels. One branch raises cyclic A M P. Another lowers it. Another raises calcium. Beta-gamma can open a potassium channel.
scenes.caption: Now the cell chooses what those surfaces meet. Follow the hourglass. Many receptors narrow to a few Gα families and βγ, then widen toward enzymes and channels. One branch raises cAMP. Another lowers it. Another raises calcium. βγ can open a potassium channel.
scenes.visual: Pull back to a full-frame hourglass labeled 'schematic'. Several differently shaped blue receptor cartoons slide into a narrow waist containing on-screen labels Gs, Gi/o, Gq/11, G12/13, and beta-gamma. Moving arrows fan out to an adenylyl-cyclase block with a rising or falling cAMP meter, a calcium store releasing dots, a Rho exchange-factor block reshaping a cell outline, and an opening potassium channel.
scenes.narration: Now the cell chooses what those surfaces meet. Follow the hourglass. Many receptors narrow to a few Gα families and βγ, then widen toward enzymes and channels. One branch raises cAMP. Another lowers it. Another raises calcium. βγ can open a potassium channel.

scenes.tts: Each family points to a main direct target, not a guaranteed exclusive partner. The receptor makes the first selection. The cell then supplies whichever enzymes, channels, and scaffolds are present. So one messenger can carry different meanings in different cells.
scenes.caption: Each family points to a main direct target, not a guaranteed exclusive partner. The receptor makes the first selection. The cell then supplies whichever enzymes, channels, and scaffolds are present. So one messenger can carry different meanings in different cells.
scenes.visual: Keep the hourglass but widen its output side to fill the frame. Place a small heading 'main targets, not exclusive'. Let one receptor send a secondary faint arrow to another family without labeling it certain. Then carry one cAMP block into two generic cell outlines that hold differently shaped downstream proteins; their response arrows point in different directions. Do not name or draw any tissue. Mark the whole picture 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Each family points to a main direct target, not a guaranteed exclusive partner. The receptor makes the first selection. The cell then supplies whichever enzymes, channels, and scaffolds are present. So one messenger can carry different meanings in different cells.

scenes.tts: The same acetylcholine can therefore meet different wiring. In a pacemaker cell, the receptor on screen loads G I, and freed beta-gamma opens potassium channels. Firing slows. In airway muscle, a different receptor loads G Q, and phospholipase C beta raises calcium. The muscle contracts. The input matches; the cellular paths differ.
scenes.caption: The same acetylcholine can therefore meet different wiring. In a pacemaker cell, the receptor on screen loads Gi, and freed βγ opens potassium channels. Firing slows. In airway muscle, a different receptor loads Gq, and phospholipase C-β raises calcium. The muscle contracts. The input matches; the cellular paths differ.
scenes.visual: Split the carried membrane into matched heart and airway cells while one identical gold acetylcholine block feeds both. Show M2 and M3 only as on-screen labels. On the heart side, teal beta-gamma opens a potassium channel and beat marks spread apart. On the airway side, purple G-alpha activates a PLC-beta block, calcium dots rise, and a muscle band shortens. Keep all pathways labeled 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: The same acetylcholine can therefore meet different wiring. In a pacemaker cell, the receptor on screen loads Gi, and freed βγ opens potassium channels. Firing slows. In airway muscle, a different receptor loads Gq, and phospholipase C-β raises calcium. The muscle contracts. The input matches; the cellular paths differ.

scenes.tts: So do not predict an answer from the ligand alone. Trace the receptor subtype, the G protein it loads, and the targets available. That path predicts the cell's first response. Dose and efficacy still change how strongly the receptor is activated. The wiring decides what that activation means.

scenes.visual: Rejoin the two cells into one left-to-right tracing tool: 'GPCR subtype' flows to 'G protein' and then 'downstream proteins', with a gold ligand entering at the start. Each block pulses in sequence while a response arrow grows. Keep a small scope label 'first response'. Then fade every object before the end card.

scenes.visual: Show one centered line only, in large high-contrast type: 'GPCR subtype, G protein, and downstream proteins decide the first response.' No logo, subtitle, or smaller line.
